nodes.title: Workflow: Scheduler Variants, Selection Rules, and DP Load Balancing
nodes.description: How vllm-ascend chooses its Ascend scheduler family at platform-config time, which combinations startup rejects, and how the balance and DyntraLB variants hook the DP engine-core busy loop to share per-rank load.
nodes.body:
# Workflow: Scheduler Variants, Selection Rules, and DP Load Balancing

vLLM v1 constructs exactly one scheduler object per engine core. vllm-ascend extends that
single object along several independent axes — cross-DP admission gating (`balance`), waiting-queue
policy (`ShortRequestFirst`), intra-decoder DP load balancing (`DyntraLB`), prefill recompute on
disaggregated decode nodes (`recompute`), profiling-driven chunk sizing (`profiling_chunk`), and
offline batch job grouping (`batch_job`) — plus one global base-class replacement. This page
covers how the variant is *chosen*, which combinations are refused at startup, and the one
correctness invariant that makes the DP load-balancing hooks safe: where the cross-rank gather
sits relative to the engine core's busy loop.

For where these flags live in the `additional_config` schema, see
[Configuration System](../architecture/configuration-system.md); for how the monkey-patches are
installed at import time, see [Patching Architecture](../architecture/patching-architecture.md).

## Two dispatch mechanisms, deliberately separate

Selection is not one mechanism. Some variants are picked by writing
`vllm_config.scheduler_config.scheduler_cls`; others are installed by rebinding a module-level
class or wrapping an entry point. The distinction matters because the second kind is *config-keyed,
not class-keyed*: it activates even if `scheduler_cls` points somewhere else.

| | Mechanism A: `scheduler_cls` assignment | Mechanism B: module-level swap / wrapper |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where | `NPUPlatform.check_and_update_config` — step 5 `_check_ascend_config` and step 8 `_setup_worker_and_scheduler` ([`platform.py`](../../vllm_ascend/platform.py#L443-L497)) | `patch_balance_schedule.py` and `patch_dyntra_lb_core.py`, imported from `vllm_ascend.patch.platform` ([`patch/platform/__init__.py`](../../vllm_ascend/patch/platform/__init__.py#L41-L42)) |
| When | Once per process, during platform config validation | At `vllm_ascend` import / `pre_register_and_update`, i.e. before any engine core exists |
| Effect | The chosen FQCN (or a replaced `SchedulerConfig` instance) travels with `VllmConfig` into the engine core and worker processes | `vllm.v1.core.sched.scheduler.Scheduler` is rebound **eagerly** to `BalanceScheduler`; `EngineCoreProc.run_engine_core` is wrapped so the `DPEngineCoreProc` symbol is swapped **conditionally** at call time |
| Applies to | The single variant the user asked for | Any config whose `scheduler_cls` is unset (Mechanism A), plus the engine-core busy loop of every DP run with the feature enabled |

Mechanism B is why balance scheduling needs no `scheduler_cls` at all: ordinary synchronous,
PD-prefill, and PD-mixed configs leave `scheduler_cls` as `None`, and upstream's construction of
`Scheduler(...)` resolves to `BalanceScheduler` because that module attribute was replaced. The patch
names its own scope — it applies "when scheduler_cls is unset, covering ordinary synchronous,
PD-prefill, and PD-mixed paths", while "recompute, dynamic-batch, and profiling schedulers set
scheduler_cls and correctly bypass this name"
([`patch_balance_schedule.py`](../../vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_balance_schedule.py#L912-L917)).
A single rebound module attribute cannot reach a class that already captured the upstream base, so
never assume the balance admission gate layered onto an explicitly selected variant.

## Selection table

`async_scheduling` below is `vllm_config.scheduler_config.async_scheduling`. "Rejected" lists only
combinations that a validator actually refuses; silently-overwritten combinations are called out in
the notes.

| Config flag | async | Chosen class | Mechanism | Required conditions | Rejected / notable combinations |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| *(nothing)* | sync | `BalanceScheduler` | B | none; balance machinery no-ops when `enable_balance_scheduling` is off | `scheduler_cls` stays `None`, so the module-level rebind decides the class |
| `enable_balance_scheduling` | sync | `BalanceScheduler` + `BalanceDPEngineCoreProc` | B | PD-mixed: `kv_transfer_config is None` or `kv_role == "kv_both"`; effectively DP > 1 for the gather | rejected with `kv_role` of `kv_producer`/`kv_consumer`; rejected with `profiling_chunk_config`; rejected with `dyntra_lb_config` |
| `enable_balance_scheduling` | async | the patch's own scope note claims only "ordinary synchronous, PD-prefill, and PD-mixed" paths | B (engine core still swaps) | same | same rejections; only `vllm.v1.core.sched.scheduler.Scheduler` is rebound, so treat the admission gate as synchronous-only and verify the constructed class rather than assuming composition |
| `short_request_first_config.enabled` | sync | *(no class)*; queue installed in `BalanceScheduler.__init__` or `ProfilingChunkScheduler.__init__` | B | `scheduler_config.policy == "fcfs"` | rejected with `batch_job_sched_config`; rejected on `kv_role="kv_consumer"`; with `profiling_chunk_config` it must be synchronous |
| `short_request_first_config.enabled` | async | `ShortRequestFirstAsyncScheduler` | A | same as above | same as above |
| `profiling_chunk_config.enabled` | either | `ProfilingChunkScheduler` (+ `patch_profiling_chunk` import) | A | `pipeline_parallel_size > 1`; `min_chunk` clamped to `max_num_batched_tokens` | rejected with `enable_balance_scheduling`; rejected with `dyntra_lb_config`; rejected with async + ShortRequestFirst |
| `batch_job_sched_config.enabled` | sync | `BatchJobAwareScheduler` | A | none enforced; intended for offline `run_batch` | rejected with `short_request_first_config` |
| `batch_job_sched_config.enabled` | async | `BatchJobAwareAsyncScheduler` | A | same | same |
| `dyntra_lb_config.enabled` and **not** `recompute_scheduler_enable` | sync | `DyntraLBScheduler` | A (+ B for the DP hook) | `kv_role == "kv_consumer"`, `data_parallel_size > 1`, `nnodes_within_dp == 1` | rejected with `enable_balance_scheduling`, `profiling_chunk_config`; not rejected with `batch_job_sched_config` (see note) |
| `dyntra_lb_config.enabled` and **not** `recompute_scheduler_enable` | async | `AsyncDyntraLBScheduler` | A (+ B) | same | same |
| `recompute_scheduler_enable`, DyntraLB off | sync | `RecomputeScheduler` | A, by **replacing** `vllm_config.scheduler_config` with `RecomputeSchedulerConfig` | `kv_role == "kv_consumer"` | rejected in PD-mixed (`kv_transfer_config is None` or `kv_both`); downgraded with a warning on `kv_producer` |
| `recompute_scheduler_enable`, DyntraLB off | async | `AsyncRecomputeScheduler` | A | same | same |
| `recompute_scheduler_enable` **and** `dyntra_lb_config.enabled` | sync | `DyntraLBRecomputeScheduler` | A | same | same |
| `recompute_scheduler_enable` **and** `dyntra_lb_config.enabled` | async | `AsyncDyntraLBRecomputeScheduler` | A | same | same |

The table is generated by two helpers that exist purely so the mapping is testable in isolation:
`_get_recompute_scheduler_cls(async_scheduling, dyntra_lb_enabled)` and
`_get_dyntra_lb_scheduler_cls(async_scheduling)`
([`platform.py`](../../vllm_ascend/platform.py#L1463-L1480),
[`test_platform.py`](../../tests/ut/test_platform.py#L286-L322),
[`test_platform.py`](../../tests/ut/test_platform.py#L1462-L1484)).

### Ordering: step 5 then step 8, last writer wins

`_check_ascend_config` (step 5) runs the policy validators and performs the two assignments that
must happen *before* anything else reads the scheduler config: the async ShortRequestFirst class
and the whole-config recompute replacement. `_setup_worker_and_scheduler` (step 8) then performs
three more assignments in a fixed order — DyntraLB, profiling chunk, batch job — each of which
overwrites `scheduler_cls` unconditionally except for DyntraLB, which is guarded by
`and not scheduler_config.recompute_scheduler_enable`
([`platform.py`](../../vllm_ascend/platform.py#L1249-L1272)). That guard is what preserves the
combined `DyntraLBRecomputeScheduler` selected in step 5.

The consequence to remember when changing anything here: **the order of the `if` blocks in step 8
is behaviour, not style, and the two phases do not share a single authority.** Step 5 can replace the
whole `SchedulerConfig`, and step 8 then overwrites `scheduler_cls` on whatever object is current. The
validators reject the colliding pairs they know about (balance × profiling chunk, balance × DyntraLB,
DyntraLB × profiling chunk, ShortRequestFirst × batch job), but the set is not exhaustive, so an
unvalidated pair fails in one of three ways rather than at startup:

- **Config and class disagree.** `batch_job_sched_config` and `profiling_chunk_config` have no role
  validator, yet either one, when enabled on a `kv_consumer` node, overwrites the recompute class
  chosen in step 5 while `recompute_scheduler_enable` stays `true` in `AscendConfig`. Config-derived
  answers such as `is_pd_decode_recompute_scheduler_enabled` then disagree with the scheduler actually
  running ([`utils.py`](../../vllm_ascend/utils.py#L1073-L1100)).
- **Attribute error at first step.** `dyntra_lb_config` × `batch_job_sched_config`: the engine-core
  hook calls `self.scheduler.prepare_dyntra_lb_step()`, which only schedulers carrying
  `DyntraLBPolicyMixin` define, while the class in use is `BatchJobAwareScheduler`
  ([`patch_dyntra_lb_core.py`](../../vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_dyntra_lb_core.py#L428-L437),
  [`dyntra_lb_scheduler.py`](../../vllm_ascend/core/dyntra_lb_scheduler.py#L242-L252)).
- **Harmless overwrite.** A pair where the later block names the variant the user actually wants is
  fine; that is how the helper-selected recompute classes survive, because the DyntraLB block is
  guarded by `and not recompute_scheduler_enable`. `profiling_chunk_config` × `batch_job_sched_config`
  is a third case: batch job wins the class, and the already-imported `patch_profiling_chunk` stays
  inert because its `EngineCore.__init__` hook only acts under
  `hasattr(self.scheduler, "run_profiling_chunk_init")`
  ([`patch_profiling_chunk.py`](../../vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_profiling_chunk.py#L197-L207)).
  Profiling is then silently unused — a no-op, not a crash.

Treat unvalidated pairs as unsupported even though startup accepts them.

### Decision diagram

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["check_and_update_config"] --> B["_check_ascend_config: policy validation"]
    B --> C{"recompute_scheduler_enable"}
    C -->|"kv_producer"| C1["warn and write back false into additional_config"]
    C -->|"kv_consumer"| C2["replace SchedulerConfig with RecomputeSchedulerConfig"]
    C -->|"no kv_transfer_config or kv_both"| C3["raise ValueError"]
    C2 --> D{"dyntra_lb_config.enabled"}
    D -->|yes| D1["DyntraLBRecomputeScheduler or Async variant"]
    D -->|no| D2["RecomputeScheduler or Async variant"]
    B --> E{"short_request_first_config.enabled and async_scheduling"}
    E -->|yes| E1["ShortRequestFirstAsyncScheduler"]
    E -->|no| E2["leave scheduler_cls unset and install queue in __init__"]
    A --> F["_setup_worker_and_scheduler"]
    F --> G{"dyntra_lb enabled and not recompute"}
    G -->|yes| G1["DyntraLBScheduler or AsyncDyntraLBScheduler"]
    G -->|no| H{"profiling_chunk_config.enabled"}
    G1 --> H
    H -->|yes| H1["ProfilingChunkScheduler plus patch_profiling_chunk import"]
    H -->|no| I{"batch_job_sched_config.enabled"}
    H1 --> I
    I -->|"async"| I1["BatchJobAwareAsyncScheduler"]
    I -->|"sync"| I2["BatchJobAwareScheduler"]
    I -->|no| J["keep current scheduler_cls"]
```

The diagram shows the two-phase write path: policy validation decides *whether* a combination is
legal and fixes up config, then a ladder of unconditional assignments decides *which* class wins.

## The variants

### Balance: a global admission gate, not a rebalancer

`enable_balance_scheduling` does not move work between ranks. Once per engine step every DP rank
all-gathers its `len(self.running)` into `self.balance_queue`; inside the WAITING loop,
`max(t.item() for t in self.balance_queue) == self.max_num_running_reqs` freezes admission on
**every** rank for that step — "any rank at cap ⇒ global freeze", so the saturated rank can drain
([`patch_balance_schedule.py`](../../vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_balance_schedule.py#L399-L416)).
Because all ranks read the same gathered vector, they reach the same decision independently; there
is no leader. The explicit anti-semantic — "make lagging ranks catch up to the leader" — is
documented as rejected in the design note
([`balance_schedule_refactor.md`](../../docs/source/developer_guide/Design_Documents/balance_schedule_refactor.md)).

`BalanceScheduler.schedule()` is a verbatim copy of the pinned vLLM release tag's `Scheduler.schedule()`
with exactly three deltas: the disabled-path early return to `super()`, the freeze gate above, and
`if request_queue is None: break` replacing upstream's `assert`
([`patch_balance_schedule.py`](../../vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_balance_schedule.py#L1-L57)).
The copy is a maintenance liability, so it is pinned to the release tag read from
`.github/vllm-release-tag.commit` (currently `v0.28.0`) and guarded by an AST-level "verbatim modulo
three deltas" test
([`test_patch_balance_schedule.py`](../../tests/ut/patch/platform/test_patch_balance_schedule.py#L481-L510)).

### ShortRequestFirst: a waiting-queue policy, installed not subclassed

The feature is a three-lane `RequestQueue` — `immediate` (recovery: preempted, or any request with
computed/output tokens), `short` (`num_prompt_tokens <= threshold`), `long` — dispatching in
`immediate > aged-long > short > long` order, with aging driven by `long_max_wait_ms`
([`short_request_first_scheduler.py`](../../vllm_ascend/core/short_request_first_scheduler.py#L37-L182)).
`peek_request` pins the selected lane so the matching `pop_request` cannot remove a different
request when aging flips lane priority between the two calls.

Installation is guarded, not defensive-by-accident: `install_short_request_first_waiting_queue`
raises if the policy is not FCFS and raises if the waiting queue is already non-empty, and is
idempotent when the queue is already installed
([`short_request_first_scheduler.py`](../../vllm_ascend/core/short_request_first_scheduler.py#L338-L367),
[`test_short_request_first_scheduler_install.py`](../../tests/ut/core/test_short_request_first_scheduler_install.py#L57-L108)).
That is why the *synchronous* path needs no class of its own: `BalanceScheduler.__init__` and
`ProfilingChunkScheduler.__init__` install the queue right after `super().__init__`, before any
request can be admitted. `ShortRequestFirstAsyncScheduler` exists only because the async path is
reached through `scheduler_cls`, so the subclass is the install hook there. `RecomputeScheduler`
deliberately does **not** install the queue, which is asserted directly
([`test_recompute_scheduler_short_request_first.py`](../../tests/ut/core/test_recompute_scheduler_short_request_first.py#L52)).

### DyntraLB: planner in the engine core, policy in the scheduler

DyntraLB targets skewed decode workloads. The load unit is a request's estimated attention KV block
count, `cdiv(len(all_token_ids), block_size)`, not its token count
([`dyntra_lb_scheduler.py`](../../vllm_ascend/core/dyntra_lb_scheduler.py#L45-L56)). Each coordinated
step, the DP engine core all-gathers a fixed-size snapshot of every rank's running and admissible
waiting block counts and runs a local planner over that shared snapshot. The planner swaps
long-for-short between the most and least loaded ranks, pulls waiting requests in while a rank is
below `max_num_seqs`, and — when no swap helps — drops the request that maximises aggregate
throughput under a fixed-overhead + per-block latency model
([`patch_dyntra_lb_core.py`](../../vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_dyntra_lb_core.py#L123-L324)).
Each rank receives its own three-field plan (`out_blk`, `in_blk`, `freeze`) and consumes it in the
next engine step.

Pausing is not preemption: `_lb_pause_request` sets `PREEMPTED` status, records the id in
`_lb_paused_req_ids`, and prepends the request to the waiting queue **without freeing its KV
blocks**, so the same rank can resume it later
([`dyntra_lb_scheduler.py`](../../vllm_ascend/core/dyntra_lb_scheduler.py#L386-L406)). The policy
lives in `DyntraLBPolicyMixin`, whose two hooks — `_apply_load_balance_modifications()` before the
running loop and `_can_admit_waiting_request()` per waiting request — are what let the same mixin be
reused by the recompute schedulers
([`dyntra_lb_scheduler.py`](../../vllm_ascend/core/dyntra_lb_scheduler.py#L242-L296)).

`mode` selects activation: `"static"` plans every step inside `[start_step, end_step)`, while
`"dynamic"` additionally waits for a newly added request whose block count exceeds
`long_req_block_threshold`, then re-arms itself only while long requests keep arriving and
self-disables after `dynamic_max_step` steps without one
([`patch_dyntra_lb_core.py`](../../vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_dyntra_lb_core.py#L403-L454)).
Arming is itself a collective — each rank contributes its pending-long-request flag and block count to
an `all_reduce(MAX)` — so all ranks enter and leave the planning window together.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> NotPlanning
    NotPlanning --> Planning: static mode inside the step window
    NotPlanning --> Planning: dynamic mode, long request armed, inside the step window
    Planning --> Planning: a new long request resets the step budget
    Planning --> NotPlanning: dynamic_max_step steps without a long request
    Planning --> NotPlanning: step_counter reaches end_step
```

Static mode skips the arming step entirely: `lb_active` then depends only on the step window. In both
modes, leaving the planning window sets `scheduler.modifications = None`, clears `lb_freeze`, and
turns off KV prefetch, so the next `schedule()` behaves like the unmodified scheduler.

The defaults are operationally surprising if you do not read them: `mode` defaults to `"dynamic"`,
`start_step` to `250`, and `end_step` to `-1` (unbounded), so enabling `dyntra_lb_config` changes
nothing for the first 250 engine steps and then only engages once a request larger than
`long_req_block_threshold` (default 700 blocks) arrives
([`ascend_config.py`](../../vllm_ascend/ascend_config.py#L1271-L1307)). Set `mode: "static"` with an
explicit window to force balancing unconditionally.

### Recompute: a replaced `SchedulerConfig`, not a patched attribute

On a disaggregated decode node, `recompute_scheduler_enable` makes preemption send the request back
to the prefill side instead of recomputing KV locally. This variant is structurally different:
`RecomputeSchedulerConfig.initialize_from_config` copies every init field off the existing
`SchedulerConfig`, sets `max_model_len`/`is_encoder_decoder`, picks the sync/async class, and
`_check_ascend_config` then assigns the new object to `vllm_config.scheduler_config`
([`recompute_scheduler.py`](../../vllm_ascend/core/recompute_scheduler.py#L67-L85),
[`platform.py`](../../vllm_ascend/platform.py#L1021-L1028)). Downstream code therefore sees a
`RecomputeSchedulerConfig`, not a mutated `SchedulerConfig`.

The recompute family is also the reason `finegrained_tp_config.oproj_tensor_parallel_size` and
`embedding_tensor_parallel_size` assert `recompute_scheduler_enable`:
their cross-DP HCCL collectives need a uniform `num_tokens` across DP ranks, which only the
recompute scheduler guarantees
([`ascend_config.py`](../../vllm_ascend/ascend_config.py#L670-L680)).

### ProfilingChunk (dynamic chunked pipeline parallel)

`ProfilingChunkScheduler` requires PP > 1 and is intended for the prefiller of a PD deployment. At
engine-core start it profiles prefill latency across descending chunk sizes through
`model_executor.collective_rpc("profile_prefill_latency", ...)`, fits a latency model, and then
substitutes a predicted chunk size for eligible prefills
([`scheduler_profiling_chunk.py`](../../vllm_ascend/core/scheduler_profiling_chunk.py#L53-L181)).
Selection is not self-contained: step 8 also imports `vllm_ascend.patch.platform.patch_profiling_chunk`,
which wraps `EngineCore.__init__` to trigger `run_profiling_chunk_init` and to wrap the scheduler's
`update_from_output`/`schedule` for online calibration. Because multiprocessing `spawn` starts a
fresh interpreter, the module also wraps `EngineCoreProc.run_engine_core` so unpickling re-applies
the patch in the child ([`patch_profiling_chunk.py`](../../vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_profiling_chunk.py#L184-L229)).

### BatchJobAware (offline batch only)

`BatchJobAwareScheduler` replaces the waiting queue with a job-grouped one: requests are grouped by
a `#job_name[...]#` tag in the request id, decode length is predicted per job by EWMA, KV blocks for
running requests are reserved ahead of time, and long/short decode jobs are prioritised depending on
whether available tokens exceed `low_available_tokens_threshold`
([`batch_job_aware_scheduler.py`](../../vllm_ascend/core/batch_job_aware_scheduler.py#L1-L39),
[`batch_job_aware_scheduler.py`](../../vllm_ascend/core/batch_job_aware_scheduler.py#L372-L408)). It documents that it
implements no starvation prevention, which is consistent with its intended offline use.

## The balance gather hook: a change-fragile invariant

This is the one placement in the scheduler stack where a reasonable-looking refactor silently
deadlocks a production engine, so it is worth stating as a rule.

**Rule.** The per-step `all_gather` of running counts must be executed by *every* DP rank on every
non-idle busy-loop iteration, and it must run immediately after the engine core's existing
cross-rank synchronization — never inside `schedule()`, and never before the idle gate.

Three facts combine to force it:

1. `all_gather` is a collective. A rank that does not call it blocks every rank that does.
2. A rank that has drained its local requests **never enters `schedule()`**; it runs a dummy batch.
   An `all_gather` living in `schedule()` would therefore be skipped by the drained rank while busy
   ranks call it — a collective mismatch that deadlocks
   ([`patch_balance_schedule.py`](../../vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_balance_schedule.py#L23-L30)).
3. `_has_global_unfinished_reqs` is itself a cross-rank collective (an internal all-reduce every 32
   steps) and the only point in the busy loop that re-synchronizes ranks on wave/idle state. It is
   also only invoked on iterations that did *not* take the idle `continue`, so every rank skips the
   gather consistently when all ranks are idle.

Hooking the gather into `_process_engine_step` instead — earlier, before that sync and before the
idle gate — decouples the gather from the synchronization: at a wave boundary one rank can reach the
gather while another is still blocked in `_process_input_queue` or `future.result()`. The
consequence is diagnosable but far from the cause: the stuck EngineCore cannot drain its worker shm
channel, the worker's `sample_tokens` response has nowhere to land, and after 60 s the engine dies
with `RPC call to sample_tokens timed out`
([`patch_balance_schedule.py`](../../vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_balance_schedule.py#L879-L898)).
The DyntraLB hook follows the same rule for the same reasons, and additionally clears the plan when
no engine is running ([`patch_dyntra_lb_core.py`](../../vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_dyntra_lb_core.py#L456-L472)).

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Busy as Busy rank
    participant Drained as Drained rank
    participant Core as DPEngineCoreProc
    Busy->>Core: engine step with a real schedule
    Drained->>Core: engine step with a dummy batch, schedule not entered
    Busy->>Core: _has_global_unfinished_reqs all-reduce
    Drained->>Core: _has_global_unfinished_reqs all-reduce
    Note over Core: both ranks just agreed on engines_running
    Busy->>Core: balance_gather all_gather of len running
    Drained->>Core: balance_gather all_gather of len running
    Note over Core: snapshot feeds the next step admission gate
```

The gather runs in both ranks even though only one of them entered `schedule()`, and it runs at the
*end* of the step — after schedule, execute, and `update_from_output` — so the snapshot it produces is
consumed by the next step's admission gate. That is precisely why it lives in the engine-core hook.

### The hook wiring, and the assumption it rests on

`BalanceDPEngineCoreProc._has_global_unfinished_reqs` calls `super()`, then injects
`self.scheduler.dp_group = self.dp_group` and calls `self.scheduler.balance_gather()`
([`patch_balance_schedule.py`](../../vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_balance_schedule.py#L863-L909)).
`balance_gather` itself returns early when balance is disabled or `dp_group` is unset, so it is safe
on every path and on DP=1 runs.

Three structural details are load-bearing and each has a drift guard:

- **Call-time name resolution.** The engine-core class is swapped by rebinding the module-level
  `DPEngineCoreProc` symbol, which works only because upstream's `run_engine_core` resolves that name
  at call time rather than binding it at import. The guard asserts the literal text
  `DPEngineCoreProc(` still appears in the original upstream function
  ([`test_patch_balance_schedule.py`](../../tests/ut/patch/platform/test_patch_balance_schedule.py#L541-L555)).
- **Conditional, not eager, engine-core swap.** `_balance_run_engine_core` installs
  `BalanceDPEngineCoreProc` only when `enable_balance_scheduling` is on, and restores the original
  otherwise; at import time `vllm.v1.engine.core.DPEngineCoreProc` is still pristine. This preserves
  "balance off ⇒ no involvement", which matters because PD-disaggregated recompute runs a different
  scheduler and must not be touched by balance machinery
  ([`patch_balance_schedule.py`](../../vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_balance_schedule.py#L919-L940)).
- **Wrapper chain order.** `patch_dyntra_lb_core` is imported after `patch_balance_schedule`, so its
  `run_engine_core` wrapper is the outer one and delegates to the balance wrapper when DyntraLB is
  off. The two features are mutually exclusive by config validation, and the chain order is asserted
  ([`test_patch_balance_schedule.py`](../../tests/ut/patch/platform/test_patch_balance_schedule.py#L563-L590)).

One asymmetry is worth knowing before adding a third engine-core hook: balance calls `super()`, while
DyntraLB calls the pristine upstream method it captured at import time
(`_ORIGINAL_HAS_GLOBAL_UNFINISHED_REQS`, bound before any swap because the `DPEngineCoreProc` symbol
is only replaced inside `run_engine_core`)
([`patch_dyntra_lb_core.py`](../../vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_dyntra_lb_core.py#L38-L38),
[`patch_dyntra_lb_core.py`](../../vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_dyntra_lb_core.py#L117-L121)). That
is harmless today only because the two features are mutually exclusive; a hook that captures the
pristine method instead of calling `super()` would silently skip the hook of any wrapper ordered
before it.

`BalanceScheduler.__init__` is also required to stay drop-in compatible with upstream's
`Scheduler.__init__`, because upstream constructs `Scheduler(...)` by keyword and after the swap that
constructs the subclass with the same kwargs; a parameter rename or shifted default breaks engine
startup rather than a test.

## PD-role restrictions, and why they exist

Several variants are only meaningful on one side of a prefill/decode split. The role is read from
`vllm_config.kv_transfer_config.kv_role`; `None` means PD-mixed (no transfer config at all).

| Variant | Allowed roles | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `enable_balance_scheduling` | PD-mixed only (`None` / `kv_both`) | It gates *admission* across co-located DP ranks that carry both prefill and decode. On a disaggregated D node the scheduler is `RecomputeScheduler`/`DyntraLBScheduler`, so balance must not engage; startup rejects `kv_producer` and `kv_consumer` explicitly |
| `short_request_first_config` | prefill or PD-mixed | It reorders *prompt* work. On a D node requests arrive with KV already computed, so the queue would fight the transfer path; startup rejects `kv_consumer` |
| `dyntra_lb_config` | `kv_consumer` only | It balances attention KV-cache load across DP ranks *inside one decode node*; there is no decode-side KV work to balance on a P node, and cross-node DP is rejected because the planner assumes one coordinated node |
| `recompute_scheduler_enable` | `kv_consumer` only | The feature *is* "on preemption, send the request back to the P node to redo prefill". On `kv_producer` it is warned about and written back to `additional_config` as `false` so worker processes (which rebuild `AscendConfig`) observe it disabled; in PD-mixed it is an error |
| `profiling_chunk_config` | intended for the P node of a PD deployment | It sizes prefill chunks from profiled prefill latency; no role validator enforces this, only PP > 1 |
| `batch_job_sched_config` | any | It is a waiting-queue policy with no KV-transfer coupling |

The `kv_producer` recompute path is a deliberate downgrade rather than an error, and it writes the
correction back into `vllm_config.additional_config` because workers reconstruct `AscendConfig` from
that dict — mutating only the parent's singleton would leave workers believing recompute is on
([`platform.py`](../../vllm_ascend/platform.py#L998-L1020)).

## Validation occurs in two layers

Some refusals happen while the `AscendConfig` tree is built, before any platform code runs; the rest
happen in `_check_ascend_config`. Knowing which layer reports an error tells you whether the failure
appears during `init_ascend_config` or during `check_and_update_config`.

| Check | Layer | Location |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `profiling_chunk` × `enable_balance_scheduling` mutex | `AscendConfig.derive_and_validate` | [`ascend_config.py`](../../vllm_ascend/ascend_config.py#L580-L585) |
| `profiling_chunk` requires `pipeline_parallel_size > 1` | `derive_and_validate` | [`ascend_config.py`](../../vllm_ascend/ascend_config.py#L573-L578) |
| `profiling_chunk.min_chunk` clamped to `max_num_batched_tokens` (warning, not error) | `derive_and_validate` | [`ascend_config.py`](../../vllm_ascend/ascend_config.py#L560-L572) |
| `finegrained_tp` requires `recompute_scheduler_enable` | `derive_and_validate` | [`ascend_config.py`](../../vllm_ascend/ascend_config.py#L670-L680) |
| `enable_balance_scheduling` role restriction | `_check_ascend_config` | [`platform.py`](../../vllm_ascend/platform.py#L925-L934) |
| ShortRequestFirst FCFS / batch-job / async-profiling / role rules | `_check_ascend_config` | [`platform.py`](../../vllm_ascend/platform.py#L938-L966) |
| DyntraLB role, DP size, single-node, balance and profiling mutexes | `_check_ascend_config` | [`platform.py`](../../vllm_ascend/platform.py#L968-L996) |
| Recompute role rules and class selection | `_check_ascend_config` | [`platform.py`](../../vllm_ascend/platform.py#L998-L1028) |

## Operating the variants

All knobs live under `additional_config.scheduler_config`; the legacy top-level scheduler keys still
resolve with a deprecation warning, and the nested form wins when both are present. `dyntra_lb_config`
is the one key with no legacy fallback — it is read only from the nested dict
([`ascend_config.py`](../../vllm_ascend/ascend_config.py#L1329-L1373)). Pick the variant from the
node's role, and pick only one *class-selecting* variant — the exception is ShortRequestFirst, which
is a queue policy and composes with a synchronous `profiling_chunk_config`
([`platform.py`](../../vllm_ascend/platform.py#L953-L957)):

```bash
# PD-mixed node: balanced admission across DP ranks
--additional-config '{"scheduler_config": {"enable_balance_scheduling": true}}'

# PD decode node: balance KV load across the DP ranks of one node
--additional-config '{"scheduler_config": {"dyntra_lb_config": {"enabled": true}}}'

# PD prefiller with PP > 1: profiling-driven chunk sizing
--additional-config '{"scheduler_config": {"profiling_chunk_config": {"enabled": true}}}'

# FCFS prefill or PD-mixed node: short-prompt priority waiting queue
--additional-config '{"scheduler_config": {"short_request_first_config": {"enabled": true, "threshold": 256}}}'
```

Two side effects are easy to mistake for bugs. `enable_balance_scheduling` has no
`data_parallel_size` validator, so a single-rank engine accepts it and simply never gathers:
`BalanceScheduler` documents `dp_group` as injected by the engine core and as meaningful only when
balance "requires DP > 1", and `balance_gather` returns early while `dp_group` is `None`
([`patch_balance_schedule.py`](../../vllm_ascend/patch/platform/patch_balance_schedule.py#L143-L170)).
And `dyntra_lb_config.enable_diagnostics=true` is a debugging aid only: it adds verbose rank-0 planner
dumps from `_print_rank_0` and per-step scheduler summaries (`print_scheduler_summary`), both of
which are deliberately gated to rank 0 or to the config flag
([`dyntra_lb_scheduler.py`](../../vllm_ascend/core/dyntra_lb_scheduler.py#L59-L116)).

## Extension points

- **A new waiting-queue policy** belongs in a `RequestQueue` subclass plus an install function with
  the same two guards as ShortRequestFirst (FCFS-only, queue empty, idempotent). Install it from the
  `__init__` of every scheduler that must support it, and pick an async subclass via `scheduler_cls`
  only when the sync path cannot reach it.
- **A new cross-rank policy** belongs in a mixin with `_apply_load_balance_modifications` /
  `_can_admit_waiting_request`-style hooks, plus an engine-core hook placed under the same rule as
  the balance gather. `RecomputeScheduler` already declares both hooks as no-ops specifically so a
  mixin can override them ([`recompute_scheduler.py`](../../vllm_ascend/core/recompute_scheduler.py#L189-L198)).
- **A new class-selection rule** goes into one of the `_get_*_scheduler_cls` helpers so the mapping
  stays unit-testable, and its `if` block goes into step 8 in the position that matches the intended
  precedence.

## Focused tests

| Test | What it pins |
| --- | --- |
| [`tests/ut/test_platform.py`](../../tests/ut/test_platform.py#L1193-L1310) | ShortRequestFirst rejections (non-FCFS, batch job, `kv_consumer`), sync + profiling-chunk acceptance, async + profiling-chunk rejection, async subclass selection |
| [`tests/ut/test_platform.py`](../../tests/ut/test_platform.py#L1427-L1618) | DyntraLB class selection, role rejection across `None`/`kv_both`/`kv_producer`, multi-node rejection, balance-on-PD rejection |
| [`tests/ut/patch/platform/test_patch_balance_schedule.py`](../../tests/ut/patch/platform/test_patch_balance_schedule.py#L481-L629) | `schedule()` drift against the pinned tag, the three deltas, `__init__` signature parity, call-time name resolution, wrapper chain order, upstream seams including `_has_global_unfinished_reqs` |
| [`tests/ut/core/test_dyntra_lb_scheduler.py`](../../tests/ut/core/test_dyntra_lb_scheduler.py) | Planner application, pause/resume, admission filtering, async variant |
| [`tests/ut/core/test_dyntra_lb_recompute_scheduler.py`](../../tests/ut/core/test_dyntra_lb_recompute_scheduler.py#L40-L63) | The combined classes really are the policy mixin plus the recompute scheduler, and both hooks are invoked from `schedule()` |
| [`tests/ut/core/test_scheduler_connector_block_state.py`](../../tests/ut/core/test_scheduler_connector_block_state.py#L17-L59) | The connector block-state handoff behaves identically across `DyntraLBScheduler`, `AsyncDyntraLBScheduler`, `BalanceScheduler`, and `ProfilingChunkScheduler` |
| [`tests/ut/core/test_short_request_first_scheduler_install.py`](../../tests/ut/core/test_short_request_first_scheduler_install.py#L57-L108) | Install guards and idempotency; async subclass installs only when enabled |
| [`tests/ut/core/test_recompute_scheduler_short_request_first.py`](../../tests/ut/core/test_recompute_scheduler_short_request_first.py#L52) | `RecomputeScheduler` keeps the upstream waiting policy |

The balance patch's own header is explicit that these CPU tests only guard reachable surfaces;
behavioural equivalence of the copied `schedule()` needs a real NPU + DP + MoE engine and lives in
e2e/nightly runs.

nodes.title: Workflow: Weight Transfer, Hot Reload, and Sleep/Wake
nodes.description: How Ascend rollout engines replace weights without a restart - the worker's init/start/update/finish lifecycle and its guards, the HCCL and NPU-IPC transfer engines with the packed-tensor wire format, the CaMemAllocator sleep levels that offload weights and discard KV cache, and the RL configuration surface that makes all of it safe.
nodes.body:
# Workflow: Weight Transfer, Hot Reload, and Sleep/Wake

Reinforcement-learning post-training needs two things from an inference engine that
serving never needs: **the weights must change while the process stays up**, and **the
NPU memory must be given back while a trainer uses the same device**. On Ascend those two
requirements are implemented by separate but coupled mechanisms:

- a **weight-transfer engine** (`hccl` or `npu_ipc`) that a trainer drives to overwrite the
  loaded model's parameters in place, and
- **sleep mode**, a pluggable allocator (`CaMemAllocator`) that can offload the weight
  memory pool to pinned host memory and unmap everything else.

They are coupled because the trainer typically needs the weights re-synchronised right
after a level-2 sleep has discarded them, and because both are gated by the same
`rl_config` switch and the same FRACTAL_NZ prohibition. This page documents both, plus
the two smaller surfaces that belong to the same feature family: the ordinary
`reload_weights` hot-reload path and the per-layer `WeightSwitchMixin` used to
reconstruct full weights inside a parallel domain.

Configuration semantics for `additional_config`/`--weight-transfer-config` live in
[The Configuration System](../architecture/configuration-system.md); the HCCL groups and
communicators that the transfer engines ride on are in
[Distributed Execution and HCCL](../integrations/distributed-and-hccl.md); plugin
registration is in [Workflow: Plugin Bootstrap](./plugin-bootstrap.md).

## Two ways to replace weights without a restart

| Path | Who drives it | Where the weights come from | Engine involved |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `collective_rpc("reload_weights")` | The controller, via RPC to every worker | A checkpoint on disk, re-read by the model loader | None |
| `init/start/update/finish_weight_update` | The trainer, over HTTP dev endpoints or `collective_rpc` | The trainer's live model tensors | `hccl` or `npu_ipc` |

The disk-based path is the simplest hot reload: update the load format, then reload.
[`examples/offline_reload_weight.py`](../../examples/offline_reload_weight.py) starts an
`LLM` with `load_format="dummy"`, calls
`collective_rpc("update_config", args=({"load_config": {"load_format": "auto"}},))` and then
`collective_rpc("reload_weights")`, and generation afterwards is coherent. `NPUWorker.reload_weights`
is a pure delegation to the model runner
([`worker.py`](../../vllm_ascend/worker/worker.py#L1250-L1252)), so it exercises the normal
loader — and therefore the normal weight post-processing — rather than a transfer engine.

Everything below concerns the second path.

## Engine registration and construction

The engines are not instantiated by the platform; they are registered as vLLM plugins and
created lazily per worker, because they need the loaded model.

`register_engine()` in the weight-transfer package registers three names with upstream
vLLM factories
([`weight_transfer/__init__.py`](../../vllm_ascend/distributed/weight_transfer/__init__.py#L24-L40)):

| Factory | Backend key | Implementation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `WeightTransferEngineFactory` (worker side) | `hccl` | `HCCLWeightTransferEngine` |
| `WeightTransferEngineFactory` (worker side) | `npu_ipc` | `NPUIPCWeightTransferEngine` |
| `WeightTransferTrainerFactory` (trainer side) | `npu_ipc` | `NPUIPCTrainerWeightTransferEngine` |

`register_engine()` is called from `vllm_ascend.register_connector()` — the same plugin
entry point that registers KV-transfer connectors
([`vllm_ascend/__init__.py`](../../vllm_ascend/__init__.py#L74-L81)). The HCCL trainer is
*not* registered in a factory: it is used through the static
`HCCLWeightTransferEngine.trainer_init` / `trainer_send_weights` pair.

On the worker, the engine is created at the end of `load_model()`, only when
`vllm_config.weight_transfer_config` is set, and it receives the `VllmConfig`, the device
and the live `model` module
([`worker.py`](../../vllm_ascend/worker/worker.py#L842-L865)):

```python
with context, set_current_vllm_config(self.vllm_config):
    self.model_runner.load_model()

if self.vllm_config.weight_transfer_config is not None:
    self.weight_transfer_engine = WeightTransferEngineFactory.create_engine(
        self.vllm_config.weight_transfer_config,
        self.vllm_config,
        self.device,
        self.model_runner.get_model(),
    )
```

Two consequences follow. First, `weight_transfer_engine` is `None` for every deployment
that did not ask for weight transfer, and the worker's public methods reject calls
instead of silently doing nothing. Second, the model-loading `context` in that snippet is
`CaMemAllocator.get_instance().use_memory_pool(tag="weights")` when sleep mode is on
([`worker.py`](../../vllm_ascend/worker/worker.py#L843-L850)) — so the same tensors the
transfer engine will later overwrite are exactly the tensors sleep mode can offload.

## The worker lifecycle contract and its guards

The worker is the state owner. It exposes four calls and enforces their order with one
boolean, `_weight_update_active`, initialised to `False` next to
`weight_transfer_engine = None`
([`worker.py`](../../vllm_ascend/worker/worker.py#L185-L188)):

| Call | Guard that can fail | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `init_weight_transfer_engine(init_info: dict)` | `_check_weight_transfer_engine` | Parses the untyped dict with `engine.parse_init_info`, then `engine.init_transfer_engine(typed_init_info)` |
| `start_weight_update()` | engine configured, not already active, `_check_nz_disabled` | `engine.start_weight_update()`, then sets `_weight_update_active = True` |
| `update_weights(update_info: dict)` | engine configured, update active | `engine.update_weights(update_info)`; on any exception clears `_weight_update_active` and re-raises |
| `finish_weight_update()` | engine configured, update active | `engine.finish_weight_update()`, then clears `_weight_update_active` |

The state machine is small enough to draw exactly
([`worker.py`](../../vllm_ascend/worker/worker.py#L310-L371)):

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Idle
    Idle --> Active: start_weight_update passes engine, reentry and NZ guards
    Active --> Active: update_weights loads one chunk
    Active --> Idle: finish_weight_update calls engine then clears flag
    Active --> Idle: update_weights raises and resets flag
    Idle --> Idle: update_weights or finish_weight_update rejected
```

*The worker's weight-update state machine: one boolean, two legal transitions, and a failure path that returns to `Idle`.*

The guards are the interesting part, because they are where misconfiguration becomes an
explicit error instead of corrupt weights:

- **`_check_weight_transfer_engine`** raises `RuntimeError("Weight transfer not configured. Please set
  weight_transfer_config to enable weight transfer.")` whenever the engine is `None`
  ([`worker.py`](../../vllm_ascend/worker/worker.py#L310-L314)). All four calls go through
  it, so a server started without `--weight-transfer-config` fails on the very first
  control-plane call rather than at the first tensor.
- **`_check_nz_disabled`** raises `ValueError` when `get_ascend_config().weight_nz_mode` is
  non-zero, and the message names both escapes: set `weight_nz_mode=0` via
  `--additional-config`, or enable `additional_config.rl_config` which forces NZ off
  ([`worker.py`](../../vllm_ascend/worker/worker.py#L323-L330)). It is called from
  `start_weight_update`, i.e. before any tensor moves.
- **Re-entry** is rejected: a second `start_weight_update` while active raises and tells
  the caller to `finish_weight_update` first; `update_weights` and `finish_weight_update`
  without an active update raise. A failed `update_weights` clears the flag so a
  half-transferred model cannot be finalised as if it were complete — the caller must
  restart the lifecycle.
- **`shutdown`** releases the engine (`engine.shutdown()`) before tearing down the model
  runner ([`worker.py`](../../vllm_ascend/worker/worker.py#L373-L386)).

Because the flags and error paths are cheap to test, they are covered directly:
`TestNPUWorkerWeightUpdate` asserts the unconfigured-engine rejection for all four calls,
the NZ rejection at start, the re-entry rejection, flag reset on engine error, double
`finish`, `update` after `finish`, and engine shutdown
([`test_worker_v1.py`](../../tests/ut/worker/test_worker_v1.py#L2048-L2185)).

### Why generation must be paused, not just started

`update_weights` blocks inside the engine: for HCCL it waits on broadcast collectives, for
NPU IPC it waits on the trainer's HTTP update call. The end-to-end tests therefore issue
the server-side `update_weights` RPC in a background thread while the trainer produces
data, and they `pause`/`resume` generation around the whole lifecycle
([`test_hccl_weight_transfer.py`](../../tests/e2e/pull_request/two_card/test_hccl_weight_transfer.py#L265-L305)).
A rollout that spans the update would mix old and new weights inside one sequence; the
`/pause` mode table in the RL guide is the operator-facing control for that.

## The HCCL engine: rendezvous then broadcast

`HCCLWeightTransferEngine` transfers weights as broadcast collectives from trainer rank 0
to every inference worker in a side process group. The lifecycle looks like this
([`hccl_engine.py`](../../vllm_ascend/distributed/weight_transfer/hccl_engine.py#L127-L214)):

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant TR as Trainer process
    participant CP as Control plane
    participant WK as NPUWorker
    participant EN as Engine
    participant MD as Model
    TR->>CP: trainer_init creates group as rank 0
    CP->>WK: init_weight_transfer_engine init_info
    WK->>EN: parse_init_info then init_transfer_engine
    EN-->>EN: StatelessProcessGroup plus PyHcclCommunicator
    TR->>CP: start_weight_update
    CP->>WK: start_weight_update
    WK->>EN: start_weight_update
    EN->>MD: initialize_layerwise_reload
    TR->>CP: update_weights update_info
    CP->>WK: update_weights
    WK->>EN: update_weights
    EN->>MD: load_weights per parameter or per packed chunk
    TR->>CP: finish_weight_update
    CP->>WK: finish_weight_update
    EN->>MD: finalize_layerwise_reload
```

*The HCCL lifecycle. The worker-side `update_weights` RPC and the trainer's broadcast must run concurrently; either side alone blocks.*

**Rendezvous and rank arithmetic.** `init_transfer_engine` builds a `StatelessProcessGroup`
plus a `PyHcclCommunicator`, with the worker's rank derived so it stays unique across data
parallel groups
([`hccl_engine.py`](../../vllm_ascend/distributed/weight_transfer/hccl_engine.py#L141-L167),
[`#L325-L339`](../../vllm_ascend/distributed/weight_transfer/hccl_engine.py#L325-L339)):

```
worker_rank = data_parallel_index * (TP * PP) + rank
rank        = worker_rank + init_info.rank_offset     # trainer occupies rank 0
```

So `HCCLWeightTransferInitInfo` carries `master_address`, `master_port`, `rank_offset`
(conventionally 1) and `world_size` (trainer + all workers), and the trainer side calls
`trainer_init` which always uses rank 0 on the current Ascend device. This is a
*stateless* group on purpose: it exists only for the data plane and never touches the
engine's global `torch.distributed` world.

**Layerwise reload hooks.** HCCL's `start_weight_update`/`finish_weight_update` are not
bookkeeping: they call upstream `initialize_layerwise_reload(self.model)` and
`finalize_layerwise_reload(self.model, self.model_config)`, which is what makes
`load_weights` accept parameters one layer at a time during the transfer. This is the
mechanism by which a transfer can be streamed without holding a second full copy of the
model.

**Receive paths.** `receive_weights` has two modes chosen by `update_info.packed`
([`hccl_engine.py`](../../vllm_ascend/distributed/weight_transfer/hccl_engine.py#L169-L209)):

- *unpacked* — for each `(name, dtype_name, shape)`, allocate an NPU tensor of that dtype
  and shape, `broadcast(..., src=0)` on the current stream, then
  `model.load_weights([(name, weight)])` and drop the reference. Simple, but one
  collective per parameter.
- *packed* — build an iterator of `(name, (shape, dtype))` and call
  `packed_broadcast_consumer(..., post_unpack_func=self.model.load_weights)`, so weights
  arrive in byte-blocks and are unpacked to typed tensors in bulk.

`HCCLWeightTransferUpdateInfo.__post_init__` validates that `dtype_names` and `shapes` have
exactly `len(names)` entries
([`hccl_engine.py`](../../vllm_ascend/distributed/weight_transfer/hccl_engine.py#L91-L102)),
which is the only schema check on this path: a trainer that omits a parameter will produce
a model with stale weights rather than an error, because `load_weights` is driven by the
names the trainer sends.

**Trainer side.** `trainer_send_weights(iterator, trainer_args)` accepts either a dict or
`HCCLTrainerSendWeightsArgs`, defaults `post_iter_func` to "extract the tensor", and then
either runs `packed_broadcast_producer` or loops `group.broadcast(tensor, src=...)` on
`args.stream or torch.npu.current_stream()`
([`hccl_engine.py`](../../vllm_ascend/distributed/weight_transfer/hccl_engine.py#L216-L272)).
The two `packed_buffer_size_bytes` / `packed_num_buffers` values must be identical on both
sides — the dataclasses document this explicitly on both `HCCLTrainerSendWeightsArgs` and
`HCCLWeightTransferUpdateInfo`.

## The NPU IPC engine: handle exchange, no rendezvous

`NPUIPCWeightTransferEngine` never talks to the trainer over a collective. The trainer
publishes *IPC handles* for its own tensors through the HTTP control plane, and the worker
rebuilds NPU tensors on top of the trainer's allocations. The consequence is a hard
topology constraint: **trainer and worker must be co-located on the same physical NPU
chip**, and the process must therefore share the device with the trainer.

`NPUIPCWeightTransferInitInfo` carries only `packed`; `init_transfer_engine` merely records
it so the worker decodes exactly what the trainer encoded, and
`start_weight_update`/`finish_weight_update` are documented no-ops (no layerwise reloading
is needed because nothing is copied per layer)
([`npu_ipc_engine.py`](../../vllm_ascend/distributed/weight_transfer/npu_ipc_engine.py#L40-L48),
[`#L153-L164`](../../vllm_ascend/distributed/weight_transfer/npu_ipc_engine.py#L153-L164)).

**Handle identity.** The two processes must agree on a key for "my chip". `npu_generate_uuid`
returns `{host_ip}-{physical_chip_id}`, where the physical chip id is the logical device
index remapped through `ASCEND_RT_VISIBLE_DEVICES` (identity mapping when the variable is
unset), and it is `lru_cache`d because it is constant for the process lifetime
([`npu_ipc_engine.py`](../../vllm_ascend/distributed/weight_transfer/npu_ipc_engine.py#L62-L90)).
This explains the test setup: the HCCL e2e test pins the server to one device, while the
NPU IPC test deliberately leaves `ASCEND_RT_VISIBLE_DEVICES` unset in the trainer so both
processes resolve to the same UUID.

**Rebuild, not copy.** On the receive side the worker:

1. takes `device_index = self.device.index` (not the ambient current device — the receive
   path is no longer wrapped in `with torch.device(...)`),
2. looks up `physical_npu_id` in the handle map and raises `ValueError` naming the
   available UUIDs if it is absent, which is the "trainer and worker are not on the same
   NPU" failure,
3. overwrites index 6 of the `reduce_tensor` args with the receiver's device index, because
   logical indices differ between the two processes,
4. calls `rebuild_npu_tensor(*args)` and finally `model.load_weights(weights)`.

For packed transfers the same steps live in `packed_npu_ipc_consumer`
([`npu_ipc_engine.py`](../../vllm_ascend/distributed/weight_transfer/npu_ipc_engine.py#L166-L222),
[`packed_tensor.py`](../../vllm_ascend/distributed/weight_transfer/packed_tensor.py#L271-L325)).
The `rebuild_npu_tensor` import is deliberately lazy: `torch_npu` is a stub on CPU CI hosts,
and the unit tests install a fake `torch_npu.multiprocessing.reductions` module to exercise
the consumer ([`test_npu_ipc_engine.py`](../../tests/ut/distributed/weight_transfer/test_npu_ipc_engine.py#L48-L62)).

**The trainer is a different class.** The static `trainer_send_weights` on the NPU IPC
engine raises `NotImplementedError` and points at
`WeightTransferTrainerFactory.trainer_init(NPUIPCTrainerInitInfo(...), client=..., source=...)`
([`npu_ipc_engine.py`](../../vllm_ascend/distributed/weight_transfer/npu_ipc_engine.py#L131-L139)).
`NPUIPCTrainerWeightTransferEngine` subclasses upstream's CUDA IPC trainer engine and
swaps the GPU primitives for NPU ones; it is constructed from a
`VLLMWeightSyncClient` and a `WeightSource`, and `send_weights()` drives the *entire*
lifecycle itself — `client.start_weight_update()`, the transfer, then
`client.finish_weight_update()` — which is why the examples and tests can call
`engine.send_weights()` and do not issue the start/finish RPCs by hand
([`npu_ipc_engine.py`](../../vllm_ascend/distributed/weight_transfer/npu_ipc_engine.py#L228-L290)).

Two correctness details in that trainer are worth knowing:

- `_all_gather_and_merge_handles` performs one `all_gather_object` of every rank's handle
  list and merges per parameter index, so a single update payload maps *every* NPU UUID to
  its rebuild args; only `is_sender` ships, the other ranks just contribute. It no-ops when
  the distributed group is absent or single-rank
  ([`npu_ipc_engine.py`](../../vllm_ascend/distributed/weight_transfer/npu_ipc_engine.py#L298-L336)).
- In unpacked mode `_send_unpacked` returns strong references to every `.contiguous()` copy,
  and `send_weights` keeps them alive until after `finish` and the post-send barrier,
  because `reduce_tensor`'s args do not keep the storage alive
  ([`npu_ipc_engine.py`](../../vllm_ascend/distributed/weight_transfer/npu_ipc_engine.py#L282-L296),
  [`#L337-L373`](../../vllm_ascend/distributed/weight_transfer/npu_ipc_engine.py#L337-L373)).
- In packed mode a barrier runs **per chunk**, because the producer reuses one IPC buffer;
  without it, another rank can overwrite the buffer while its co-located worker is still
  reading the previous chunk
  ([`npu_ipc_engine.py`](../../vllm_ascend/distributed/weight_transfer/npu_ipc_engine.py#L375-L398)).

## The packed-tensor wire format shared by both engines

Both backends speak the same encoding, implemented once in
[`packed_tensor.py`](../../vllm_ascend/distributed/weight_transfer/packed_tensor.py):

1. each tensor is made contiguous and reinterpreted as a flat `uint8` view;
2. tensors are appended to a buffer until the byte budget is exceeded
   (`DEFAULT_PACKED_BUFFER_SIZE_BYTES = 1 GiB`, `DEFAULT_PACKED_NUM_BUFFERS = 2`);
3. the consumer splits the block by the recorded per-tensor byte sizes and views each slice
   back to `dtype` and `shape`.

The metadata that travels with a block is therefore `names`, `dtype_names`, `shapes` and
`tensor_sizes` (plus, for NPU IPC, the handle that carries the bytes). The invariant that
matters operationally: **`buffer_size_bytes` and `num_buffers` are part of the protocol, not
a local tuning knob** — producer and consumer must agree, and the HCCL dataclasses say so
in their docstrings
([`packed_tensor.py`](../../vllm_ascend/distributed/weight_transfer/packed_tensor.py#L12-L38),
[`#L114-L127`](../../vllm_ascend/distributed/weight_transfer/packed_tensor.py#L114-L127)).

The two engines realize the buffering differently:

| Aspect | HCCL `packed_broadcast_*` | NPU IPC `packed_npu_ipc_*` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Buffers | `num_buffers` fresh `uint8` tensors, one dedicated NPU stream each | one reusable buffer allocated once and registered for IPC once |
| Overlap | producer packs on stream *i* while the consumer unpacks and calls `load_weights` on its stream *i* | producer fills, synchronizes, yields a chunk; consumer rebuilds, copies out, clones |
| Flow control | stream synchronizations before/after each broadcast | per-chunk barrier on the trainer plus `torch.npu.current_stream().synchronize()` before yielding |
| Failure mode guarded | exit-time hang from in-flight work (final synchronize of all streams) | silent corruption from buffer reuse (consumer `.clone()`s every tensor) |

Concretely, `packed_npu_ipc_producer` raises `ValueError` when a single tensor is larger
than `buffer_size_bytes` (the only hard sizing error in the format), and
`packed_npu_ipc_consumer` clones each unpacked tensor precisely because the producer reuses
the buffer across chunks
([`packed_tensor.py`](../../vllm_ascend/distributed/weight_transfer/packed_tensor.py#L231-L258),
[`#L313-L325`](../../vllm_ascend/distributed/weight_transfer/packed_tensor.py#L313-L325)).
`tests/ut/distributed/weight_transfer/test_packed_tensor.py` validates the
pack/unpack round-trip on CPU tensors with `torch.npu` stubbed out, which is the cheapest
regression net for a byte-level format.

## Sleep mode: what is offloaded, what is discarded

Sleep mode is implemented by `CaMemAllocator` in
[`camem.py`](../../vllm_ascend/device_allocator/camem.py), a singleton around a
`torch.npu.memory.NPUPluggableAllocator` backed by the `vllm_ascend_C` extension
(`init_module`, `python_create_and_map`, `python_unmap_and_release`, and `acl.rt.memcpy`).
It must be a singleton because the C extension stores the free callback in a global
variable ([`camem.py`](../../vllm_ascend/device_allocator/camem.py#L113-L149)). If the
extension cannot be imported, sleep mode is disabled with a warning at import time.

Every allocation made inside `use_memory_pool(tag)` is recorded as
`AllocationData(handle, tag)`. Only two tags are created by the worker:

| Tag | Created in | Contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `weights` | `load_model`, wrapping `model_runner.load_model()` | model parameters and buffers |
| `kv_cache` | `initialize_from_config`, wrapping `model_runner.initialize_kv_cache()` | KV-cache tensors |

`CaMemAllocator.sleep(offload_tags)` then does the following for each recorded allocation
([`camem.py`](../../vllm_ascend/device_allocator/camem.py#L180-L226)):

- skip anything tagged `sleep_persistent` — that tag is never offloaded and never unmapped,
  so it survives sleep/wake cycles for free;
- if the allocation's tag is in `offload_tags`, copy the bytes to a pinned host tensor with
  `ACL_MEMCPY_DEVICE_TO_HOST` and remember it as `cpu_backup_tensor`;
- unmap and release the device allocation **in every case**, then `gc.collect()` and
  `torch.npu.empty_cache()`.

So "offload" and "discard" differ only in whether a host copy exists. `wake_up(tags)`
remaps each allocation whose tag is selected (all of them when `tags is None`) and copies
the host backup back when present
([`camem.py`](../../vllm_ascend/device_allocator/camem.py#L227-L254)).

### The two levels

`NPUWorker.sleep(level)` maps the level onto `offload_tags`
([`worker.py`](../../vllm_ascend/worker/worker.py#L250-L279)):

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S["worker.sleep level"] --> L1{"level is 1"}
    L1 -->|yes| W1["save only allowed control buffers to CPU, then allocator.sleep with offload_tags weights"]
    L1 -->|no| W2["save every named buffer to CPU, then allocator.sleep with empty offload_tags"]
    W1 --> R1["weights copied to pinned host memory, kv_cache unmapped"]
    W2 --> R2["weights and kv_cache both unmapped, no host copy"]
    R1 --> X{"rl_config enabled and sleep_mode_extra_cleanup"}
    R2 --> X
    X -->|yes| EX["clear ACL graph workspaces, reset graph params, drain PP sends, destroy HCCL groups"]
    X -->|no| DONE["sleep returns and logs freed bytes"]
```

*Level 1 offloads weights and discards KV cache; level 2 discards both; extra cleanup is an independent opt-in.*

- **Level 1** keeps the weights recoverable on the host and forgets the KV cache. The
  documented use case is "reuse the same model later" — cheap wake-up, at the cost of CPU
  memory equal to the weight footprint.
- **Level 2** passes an empty `offload_tags` tuple, so nothing is copied and everything is
  unmapped: the model's parameters have no valid storage until something reloads them.
  This is the level that pairs with weight transfer (or `reload_weights`).

After the allocator call the worker asserts `freed_bytes >= 0` ("Memory usage increased
after sleeping.") and logs freed and still-used GiB, which is the only built-in sanity
check that a level actually returned memory.

### Buffers saved outside the weight mem-pool

Not every tensor that must survive a sleep lives in the `weights` pool. The worker keeps
`self._sleep_saved_buffers: dict[str, torch.Tensor]` and copies named buffers to CPU before
handing memory to the allocator
([`worker.py`](../../vllm_ascend/worker/worker.py#L117-L123),
[`#L253-L260`](../../vllm_ascend/worker/worker.py#L253-L260)):

- **Level 1** saves only buffers whose *trailing* name segment is in `_allowed_names`, which
  is currently `("_dsa_cp_hadamard", "_dsa_hadamard")`. The comment on that tuple states the
  reason: these control buffers are created **outside** the weights mem-pool, so level-1
  sleep would otherwise destroy them while keeping the rest of the model.
- **Level 2** saves *all* named buffers, since the pool is discarded wholesale — which is
  also why MoE code promotes runtime NPU state (`log2phy`, `moe_load`, `load_counter`) to
  registered buffers with the comment "Level-2 sleep discards NPU tensors that are not
  parameters/buffers"
  ([`routed_experts.py`](../../vllm_ascend/ops/fused_moe/routed_experts.py#L490-L510)).

`wake_up` restores them by copying into the live buffers and then clears the dict
([`worker.py`](../../vllm_ascend/worker/worker.py#L293-L299)). Because the dict is cleared
on the *first* wake-up call, buffers are restored at that point regardless of which tag was
woken — relevant for the two-phase level-2 sequence.

### `wake_up` and FRACTAL_NZ

`wake_up(tags)` starts with a hard check that mirrors `_check_nz_disabled`
([`worker.py`](../../vllm_ascend/worker/worker.py#L281-L299)):

```python
nz_mode = get_ascend_config().weight_nz_mode
if nz_mode:
    raise ValueError(
        "FRACTAL_NZ mode is enabled. This may cause model parameter precision issues "
        "in the RL scenarios. Please set weight_nz_mode=0 via --additional-config, "
        "or enable additional_config.rl_config (enabled: true) which disables NZ "
        "automatically."
    )
```

The code's stated reason is precision: in an RL loop the restored weights are consumed by
(or overwritten from) a trainer, and the NZ-cast layout that
`process_weights_after_loading`/`maybe_trans_nz` produces for each layer is not what the
reload path writes back
([`ops/linear.py`](../../vllm_ascend/ops/linear.py#L91-L107),
[`utils.py`](../../vllm_ascend/utils.py#L276-L304)). Since `weight_nz_mode` defaults to `1`,
this means a sleep/wake deployment must opt out of NZ explicitly, either through
`additional_config.weight_nz_mode: 0` or through `rl_config.enabled: true`. The same rule is
enforced at `start_weight_update`, so the two halves of the RL loop agree.

After the check, `wake_up` runs `allocator.wake_up(tags=tags)`, restores the saved buffers,
optionally calls `model_runner.post_kv_cache_wake_up()` on vLLM `0.28.0` when `tags` is
`None` or contains `"kv_cache"`, and finally runs the extra-cleanup wake-up when enabled.
The tag ordering contract is the documented two-phase sequence: wake `weights`, load or
transfer new weights, then wake `kv_cache`.

### Extra cleanup (`rl_config.sleep_mode_extra_cleanup`)

By default sleep touches only allocator-managed memory. For same-NPU RL deployments where
the trainer needs the device back, an opt-in path releases two more resources, implemented
in [`sleep_mem_optimized.py`](../../vllm_ascend/device_allocator/sleep_mem_optimized.py)
and gated in the worker by `rl_config.enabled and rl_config.sleep_mode_extra_cleanup`
([`worker.py`](../../vllm_ascend/worker/worker.py#L262-L266),
[`#L301-L309`](../../vllm_ascend/worker/worker.py#L301-L309)):

| Phase | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| sleep | `AclGraphSleepWakeupManager`: clear attention workspaces in `_graph_params`/draft graph params, empty the list-valued graph fields, clear the model runner's cudagraph manager. Then `HcclSleepWakeupManager`: wait pending `_pp_send_work` handles, `torch.npu.synchronize()`, `destroy_hccl()` on every alive `GroupCoordinator` |
| wakeup | `restore_hccl()` + `refresh_moe_hccl_groups()`, then `capture_model()` again — but only when `tags is None` or contains `"kv_cache"` |

The ACL-first, HCCL-second ordering is asserted by a unit test, as is the "skip ACL graph
sleep when ACL graph is disabled" case and the `kv_cache`-gated recapture
([`test_sleep_mem_optimized.py`](../../tests/ut/device_allocator/test_sleep_mem_optimized.py#L54-L107)).
The `capture_model()` gate is the important operational invariant: level-2 wake restores
weights *before* an external load, so recapturing graphs at that moment would bake in
not-yet-loaded weights. `restore_hccl` recreates the group in place through the patched
`GroupCoordinator`
([`patch_distributed.py`](../../vllm_ascend/patch/worker/patch_distributed.py#L234-L250)).

The trade-off is explicit in the docs and visible in the code: extra cleanup lowers
sleep-time NPU usage and lengthens wake-up (HCCL re-init plus graph recapture).

## The RL configuration surface

All of this is configured through `additional_config.rl_config`, whose `apply()` method
turns the master switch into a set of fixed behaviours
([`ascend_config.py`](../../vllm_ascend/ascend_config.py#L253-L285)):

| Field | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled` | `false` | Forces `weight_nz_mode = 0` (warning if it was not), removes `expandable_segments` from `PYTORCH_NPU_ALLOC_CONF`, sets `VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE=1` |
| `sleep_mode_extra_cleanup` | `false` | Enables the HCCL/ACL-graph cleanup path described above; ignored unless `enabled` |
| `enable_training_consistency` | `false` | Selects the FA3 attention backend for train/infer consistency |
| `enable_batch_invariant` | `false` | Sets `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` |

`apply()` runs at the end of `init_ascend_config`, after `derive_and_validate`, and the
`rl_config` sub-dict also forces a config refresh on every initialisation
([`ascend_config.py`](../../vllm_ascend/ascend_config.py#L1474-L1483),
[`#L1567-L1569`](../../vllm_ascend/ascend_config.py#L1567-L1569)).

The documented mutual exclusions follow from the allocator implementation:

- **`expandable_segments` and sleep mode cannot coexist.**
  `CaMemAllocator.__init__` asserts `"expandable_segments:True" not in PYTORCH_NPU_ALLOC_CONF`
  with a link to the upstream PyTorch issue
  ([`camem.py`](../../vllm_ascend/device_allocator/camem.py#L151-L158)). That is why
  `_set_pytorch_npu_alloc_env` skips the usual `expandable_segments:True` default whenever
  `enable_sleep_mode` is set
  ([`platform.py`](../../vllm_ascend/platform.py#L1310-L1338)), and why `rl_config.apply()`
  strips it again for RL deployments.
- **Sleep mode allows one pool per process.** `load_model` asserts
  `allocator.get_current_usage() == 0` with "Sleep mode can only be used for one instance
  per process."
- **FRACTAL_NZ is incompatible with both halves of the loop.** `rl_config` forces it off,
  `start_weight_update` and `wake_up` reject it, and `wake_up`'s message names `rl_config`
  as the fix.
- **Sleep mode is not available everywhere** — the 310P MRv2 model runner raises
  `NotImplementedError("Sleep mode is not supported by model runner v2 on 310P.")`
  ([`_310p/worker/v2/model_runner.py`](../../vllm_ascend/_310p/worker/v2/model_runner.py#L99-L105)).

The user-facing command lines, endpoint list and pause-mode table are in the repository's
RL and sleep-mode guides; this page is the implementation view of the same machinery.

## Weight-switch linears: local versus full weights per layer

`WeightSwitchMixin` in [`weight_switch/linear.py`](../../vllm_ascend/weight_switch/linear.py)
is a different problem from weight transfer: it is about a *single layer* needing two
views of its own weights. Some attention-path kernels (DSA-CP, SFA-PCP O-projection) want
the full weight for prefill while the layer's parameters are sharded across a parallel
domain for decode. The mixin gives a linear method the ability to switch a layer's tensor
attributes between the sharded local view and an all-gathered full view, in place, using
`tensor.set_()` so no other code has to know
([`linear.py`](../../vllm_ascend/weight_switch/linear.py#L146-L182),
[`#L523-L538`](../../vllm_ascend/weight_switch/linear.py#L523-L538)).

Its contract is declarative:

| Piece | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `weight_switch_gather_specs` / `weight_switch_repeat_specs` | Attributes to all-gather (input-sharded layers) or repeat locally |
| `weight_switch_output_gather_specs` / `weight_switch_output_repeat_specs` | The same for output-sharded layers |
| `supports_weight_switch` | The single opt-in gate used by callers; `False` by default, set per quantization method |
| `WeightSwitchConfig` | The caller-selected parallel domain: `group`, `world_size`, `rank`, optional `shard_axis`; validated as `0 <= rank < world_size` |
| `WeightLoadPartition` | An independent checkpoint partition, composed from nested groups as `outer * inner` world size and `outer_rank * inner_size + inner_rank` |

`_get_weight_switch_specs` infers the axis from the layer (`input_size != input_size_per_partition`
⇒ input-sharded, likewise for output) and raises if *both* axes are pre-sharded, or if the
layer is unsharded and `config.shard_axis` was not given. `enable_weight_switch` allocates
full-size buffers (optionally from a shared `pool` keyed by attr/dtype/device/dim/shape),
clones local tensors when asked, and records `WeightSwitchState`; `all_gather_weight`
launches `all_gather_async` per attribute and refuses to launch a second gather while
`state.handles` is non-empty, so callers must `wait_weight_all_gather` first. The quantized
methods advertise their specs next to their kernels, e.g.
[`w8a8_dynamic.py`](../../vllm_ascend/quantization/methods/w8a8/w8a8_dynamic.py#L61-L74).

`prepare_layer_for_parallel_weight_load` is the loader half: it resizes each input-sharded
parameter to the composed shard width and installs a replacement `weight_loader` that
narrows exactly one checkpoint slice, restoring the original `tp_rank`/`tp_size` for v2
parameters so the layer's forward TP metadata is untouched. It refuses double installation
and requires `weight_loader` on every input-sharded parameter
([`linear.py`](../../vllm_ascend/weight_switch/linear.py#L259-L392)). `OProjWeightSwitchMixin`
wraps all of this into a small lifecycle for one `o_proj` (enable, all-gather, "use full
weights" context manager that always switches back)
([`o_proj.py`](../../vllm_ascend/weight_switch/o_proj.py#L13-L83)), and both the DSA-CP and
SFA-PCP implementations guard on `isinstance(linear_method, WeightSwitchMixin) and
linear_method.supports_weight_switch`, raising otherwise
([`sfa_cp.py`](../../vllm_ascend/attention/context_parallel/sfa_cp.py#L53-L85)).

This surface does not move weights between processes; it is orthogonal to the transfer
engines and is *not* used by the RL weight-sync path. It is included here because it is the
third mechanism in the codebase that rewrites live model parameters in place, and because
its `supports_weight_switch` gate and `set_()`-aliasing invariant are the things a new
quantization method must get right before either mechanism can be trusted on that method.

## Failure modes worth recognising

| Symptom | Cause | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Weight transfer not configured. Please set weight_transfer_config ...` | `--weight-transfer-config` missing, so the engine was never created | `_check_weight_transfer_engine` |
| `FRACTAL_NZ mode is enabled ...` on start or wake | `weight_nz_mode` is 1 or 2 (the default is 1); either set it to 0 or enable `rl_config` | `_check_nz_disabled`, `wake_up` |
| `start_weight_update called while a weight update is already active` | A previous update was never finished (or its `finish` failed) | worker state machine |
| `start_weight_update must be called before update_weights` | Chunks sent without opening the lifecycle — or sent after a chunk raised, since the failure resets the flag | worker state machine |
| `HCCL weight transfer not initialized. Call init_transfer_engine() first.` | `receive_weights` before the rendezvous | `HCCLWeightTransferEngine.receive_weights` |
| `IPC handle not found for NPU UUID ...` | Trainer and worker are not on the same physical NPU chip (different `ASCEND_RT_VISIBLE_DEVICES`) | `npu_ipc_engine` |
| `ValueError: Tensor '...' has size N bytes, which exceeds buffer_size_bytes` | A single tensor is larger than the packed buffer | `packed_npu_ipc_producer` |
| `Expandable segments are not compatible with memory pool.` | `PYTORCH_NPU_ALLOC_CONF` still has `expandable_segments:True` while sleep mode is on | `CaMemAllocator.__init__` |
| `Sleep mode can only be used for one instance per process.` | A second `LLM`/engine built in the same process with sleep mode | `load_model` |
| `Memory usage increased after sleeping.` | The allocator released nothing (wrong tag, or work still in flight) | `NPUWorker.sleep` |
| Silent stale weights after a "successful" HCCL update | The trainer's name list omitted parameters; `load_weights` only loads what it is given | `receive_weights` |
